origin_region: Across Europe (the black elder grows wild from Britain to the Balkans); commercial dried flowers come mainly from Bulgaria, Poland and Hungary
cultivar: Sambucus nigra (black elder); flowers only, picked as whole flat heads
processing: Flat flower heads are picked on a dry, sunny morning when fully open, dried quickly in shade, and the florets are rubbed from the stalks and sifted, because the green stalks are bitter; no fermentation.
harvest_season: Two to three weeks from late May to June, in dry weather; the whole year's supply is dried then. The berries come in September and are a separate product.
appearance_dry: Tiny cream-yellow dried florets and loose pollen with a few fine stalks, smelling musky and sweet.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold, slightly hazy with pollen.
appearance_wet: Softened cream florets with a muscat-grape scent.
taste_profile: Sweet, muscat-grape and honey florals with a musky, slightly green edge and a dry finish; it turns bitter if the steep runs long or the stalks were left in.

brewing.notes: A heaped tablespoon of florets per cup (they weigh nothing), water just under the boil, 5 minutes with a lid; longer and it goes bitter. Honey and lemon suit it, and it is the classic partner for linden, peppermint and elderberry.

vintage_note: Sold as the current summer's harvest and best within a year: fresh elderflower is cream-coloured and smells of muscat, old elderflower is brown and smells of dust. In Central Europe it is sold as a pharmacy herb with a harvest year on the box, in Britain more often by tea merchants without a date; elderflower cordial and syrups are a separate product. Look for sifted florets with as little green stalk as possible.
description:
Elderflower is the smell of early summer in a European hedgerow: flat creamy flower heads with a sweet, musky, muscat-grape scent that goes into cordials, sparkling drinks and, dried, into one of the oldest herbal teas on the continent. The British know it mostly as a cordial, the Germans and Austrians as Holunderblütentee, Eastern Europeans as a pharmacy herb for colds.

The flowers are picked on a dry morning when fully open and dried fast in shade; speed matters because they brown within a day if damp, and the florets are then rubbed off the bitter green stalks. A good pack is pale cream and almost all florets; a poor one is yellow-brown and full of stalk.

Brewed five minutes with water just under the boil, it is sweet, floral and honeyed with a faint green mustiness and a dry finish, light in body and easy to drink. Over-steeping makes it bitter, as do stalks, and that is where most disappointing cups come from. Honey and lemon are the usual additions, and it blends beautifully with linden, peppermint and lemon balm; elderflower with dried elderberries is a classic winter blend.

Buy sifted florets from the latest summer, check the colour and smell, and look for a harvest year if the shop or pharmacy gives one. There is no grading beyond that, and nothing to fake.

It has traditionally been drunk hot for colds and fevers; whatever you make of that, it is a lovely spring-scented cup and a good one to cold-brew with a slice of lemon in summer.
sources_note: origin_country is a judgement call; elderflower tea is traditional across all of Europe.
